First, an apology: although I work in acoustics and write answers and popular science articles, I really don’t know much about headphones, speakers and hi-fi, and a lot of the jargon is lost on me. I don’t particularly like or study headphones. I do like speakers, though: as long as they’re loud and the subwoofer booms, I’m happy. So there’s only so much I can say.

Second, we all come from science and engineering, so we’re relatively objective and rational, and there’s no need to go at each other. Stick to the facts. If you want drama, go watch a palace-intrigue soap; if you want to get personal, arrange a fistfight; and if you can settle it with your fists, skip the trash talk (am I stirring things up? No, not at all).

So here are just a few thoughts of mine.

Acoustics is special as a discipline: its results can be seen with your eyes, but also heard with your ears. That gives rise to an important branch of the field, psychoacoustics.

(Hey there, buddy! Come on in, start with a couple of grilled kidney skewers:)

A history of acoustics: psychoacoustics, part 1A history of acoustics: psychoacoustics, part 2

In psychoacoustics, sound is evaluated both subjectively and objectively.

On the objective side, there are the classic sound pressure level and A-weighted sound pressure level, and, later, the psychoacoustic parameters: loudness, roughness, sharpness, fluctuation strength, tonality and so on and so forth. Each psychoacoustic parameter has more than one model for computing it, but in the end they can all be calculated from formulas. A sound source, a sensor (a microphone), record the signal, compute the result.

Now for subjective evaluation. A person has two ears, which are like two microphones, and the principle is similar: a source emits sound, which travels down the ear canal to the eardrum and then on to the cochlea. The basilar membrane in the cochlea opens MATLAB and starts running Fourier transforms, and sounds of different frequencies are picked up at different places along it. This is where sound undergoes its metamorphosis, from a mechanical signal into an electrochemical one that is sent to the brain. I’ve written about this in detail in another answer, so I won’t repeat it here.

How do we perceive how high or low a sound is?

So here’s the question: what happens once it reaches the brain? Sorry, it seems not many people know yet.

In acoustics, the most common method of subjective evaluation is to run listening tests with large numbers of people. Since you can’t open up a brain to look at the parts, you have to infer how it works from what it shows on the outside. And there’s… an awful lot going on there.

The same person can give completely different results on different days, or at different times of day. Even if that person were an AI from Westworld, with every setting under tight control, what if it became self-aware and stopped answering properly? A typical listening test takes at least twenty minutes, and long ones run to an hour. How do you keep a black box like a human under control? I’ve been the guinea pig in no fewer than fifty listening tests. Sometimes I looked at my phone, sometimes my mind went blank, sometimes I gazed at the sky, sometimes I drifted back to that run into the sunset, the youth I’ve lost, and sometimes… I did answer the questions seriously.

OK, suppose humans were perfect and answered obediently 100% of the time. Would the problem go away? How you design the questions in a subjective test matters too! The simplest example: for ratings you might use 1–5, 1–10, 1–100 or 1–N. If you build software for subjective evaluation, do people drag a slider between 1 and N, or type in a number? How many decimal places? Do you need a logarithmic or exponential scale? I have no idea, because I don’t understand myself! I wish my perception could be measured in numbers too; then you’d just tweak away and be done with it!

Of course, subjective evaluation isn’t only about numbers; some studies use words to describe perception. But again: hasn’t everyone had moments when words fail them?

Some researchers have now started bringing EEG into acoustics, to see how sound affects the brain’s electrical activity. But strictly controlling the variables is still hard.


Now someone will say: why not study the correlation between subjective perception and objective parameters? Exactly. I naively said so, and then did it. I built a neural network model: record a sound, compute a few psychoacoustic parameters, and predict how annoying people will find it. I recruited lots of people for listening tests, recorded all sorts of sounds and had them rate how annoying each one was. Some results came out of it, but when you’ve built a model like that yourself, you know exactly how far it can be trusted. Some neural network gurus may tell me I had too few hidden layers or chose the weights badly. If so, let’s talk, and if we get results, we’ll publish together!

So is subjective evaluation useless? Of course not.

In a field as niche as acoustics, psychoacoustics is a very important part, and many researchers keep pushing the discipline forward through subjective evaluation, listening tests and large-scale data analysis. Many of the results also help the public understand hearing and the ear better and give real guidance, especially from listening tests that are carefully designed, choose their participants rigorously and analyze their data soundly.

It’s just that subjective evaluation research, as it stands, still doesn’t convince many people. A good share of acousticians don’t accept listening tests, or even look down on them as nonsense. I understand that: after all those years of speaking in formulas and in zeros and ones, black or white, what on earth is doing science with your ears supposed to be?

Having run listening tests and subjective evaluations and taken part in them, I know the pitfalls all too well, and I certainly can’t trust their results completely. But as I said, subjective evaluation provides guidance. If 10,000 people say headphone A is better than headphone B, there’s probably something to it. But that’s more on the qualitative level, not the quantitative one. You might be person number 10,001.

Buying headphones? Go and try them. If they feel right and you can afford them, buy them!


To finish, a little sentiment. Below is an exchange between two founding fathers of acoustics, from Helmholtz’s review of Rayleigh’s Theory of Sound:

“...Lord Rayleigh certainly deserves the thanks of all physicists and students of physics. He has rendered them a great service by what he has done hitherto. But I believe I am speaking in the name of all of them if I express the hope, that the difficulties of that which yet remains still incite him to crown his work by completing it.”
Lord Rayleigh’s Theory of Sound [A review by Hermann von Helmholtz, Nature 19, 117–118 (Dec. 12, 1878)]

So what I want to say is: see that? Back then you could get a book review into Nature!

Just kidding. What I really want to say is: aren’t they adorable together!
